12:36/q01 How does the verse indicate Joseph's imprisonment? [وَدَخَلَ ٱلسِّجْنَ · rhetoric]
  12:36/q01/p1 It leaves his imprisonment unstated and implies it through the youths' entry with him. — reasons: Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi identify the omitted prior event, 'they imprisoned him'; Ibn al-Jawzi relays al-Zajjaj.
  12:36/q01/p2 The wording itself shows Joseph was already imprisoned. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj says entry into prison with him establishes his imprisonment; al-Wahidi reports the inference.
12:36/q02 What does 'with him' say about when the youths entered? [مَعَهُ · grammar] (turns on: Whether maʿa requires concurrence when the entry began.)
  12:36/q02/p1 They entered prison together with Joseph at the same time. — reasons: Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take maʿa as newly begun companionship; Abu Hayyan says it denotes a new shared event; al-Biqaʿi cites him. Al-Alusi prefers concurrence as the original sense, while comparing 27:44.
  12:36/q02/p2 The wording allows different times; it only establishes shared confinement. — reasons: Ibn ʿAtiyya allows simultaneous or separate admission. Al-Qurtubi allows before, after or together and says the verse only requires the same room.
12:36/q03 Why place 'with him' before 'prison,' and what might the wording imply? [مَعَهُ ٱلسِّجْنَ · rhetoric] (turns on: The force of maʿa and the emphasis conveyed by word order.)
  12:36/q03/p1 The order emphasizes companionship, with Joseph as the focus. — reasons: Al-Alusi says the object precedes the subject for emphasis and companionship precedes prison because it matters more; he cites 18:62. He distinguishes ongoing Islam from punctual entry and invokes 27:44.
  12:36/q03/p2 Their entry with him may have made imprisonment easier through his presence. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports this possibility.
  12:36/q03/p3 The expression associates Joseph with their prison state while leaving his choice of it unstated. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports this explanation and observes that maʿa normally implies concurrence from the action's beginning.
  12:36/q03/p4 'With' can express joining another in obedience rather than exact simultaneous action. — reasons: Al-Kashf's comparison is the Queen's 'I submitted with Solomon' (27:44): she enters submission to God and the Messenger following prophetic guidance, despite earlier religious self-understanding.
12:36/q04 How is 'prison' pronounced and understood here? [ٱلسِّجْنَ · readings] (turns on: The vocalization and whether the noun denotes place or act.)
  12:36/q04/p1 With kasra, it means the place of confinement. — reasons: Ibn ʿAshur says all readers use kasra because one enters a place, not the act of imprisoning.
  12:36/q04/p2 With fatḥa, al-sajn denotes the prison location. — reasons: Al-Alusi gives this vocalization in explaining the clause after implied 'they imprisoned him.'
12:36/q05 Why are the prisoners called 'two youths'? [فَتَيَانِ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the designation concerns age, service status or their mutual conduct.)
  12:36/q05/p1 Fatā can designate an enslaved man or servant regardless of age. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj allows young or old slaves; al-Mawardi says slaves are so called; al-Qushayri also permits free servants; Ibn ʿAtiyya allows literal youth, slave, or free servant. Ibn al-Anbari ties it to being owned. Al-Tabataba'i takes them as young male slaves.
  12:36/q05/p2 They are called youths because neither tried to outdo the other's claim and each deferred to his companion. — reasons: Al-Tustari gives this ethical explanation.
12:36/q06 What is the form of 'two youths'? [فَتَيَانِ · grammar]
  12:36/q06/p1 It is the dual of fatā, a weak-y noun. — reasons: Al-Nahhas identifies the dual; al-Qurtubi notes the irregular form al-futu.
12:36/q07 Who were the two prisoners and whom did they serve? [فَتَيَانِ · referent] (turns on: Whether external reports are used to fill the Quran's unnamed roles.)
  12:36/q07/p1 They were the Egyptian king's baker or food steward and cupbearer or wine steward. — reasons: Qatada, Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and many commentators assign food and drink duties; the wine vision belongs to the cupbearer and bread vision to the baker. Ibn ʿAshur says the Quran leaves offences unspecified; Asad cites the Bible for the offices; Islahi stresses that the Quran does not identify them. Al-Razi says Joseph could infer royal service from their later use of rabb for their master in 12:41-42.
  12:36/q07/p2 The Quran leaves their identities unnamed. — reasons: Islahi states this limitation explicitly; Asad says the Bible identifies the offices without conflict with the Quran.
12:36/q08 What names are reported for the king and the two servants? [فَتَيَانِ · reports] (turns on: The transmitted personal names differ beyond spelling variants.)
  12:36/q08/p1 Ibn Ishaq's pair is Majlath or Mujlith and Nabu or Nabwa; the latter serves drink. — reasons: The names vary in spelling: Mujlith/Majlath/Mujlab and Nabu/Nabwa/Banu/Bunū. King-name order varies: al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid or al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan; Baghawi adds ibn Sharwan. Al-Suhayli could not retain the baker's name.
  12:36/q08/p2 The servants were Sharham Aqam and Sharham Asham. — reasons: Muqatil gives these fuller names.
  12:36/q08/p3 The cupbearer was Manja and the baker Majlath. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi cites Kaʿb via al-Thaʿlabi.
  12:36/q08/p4 They were Sharham and Sarham. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi cites al-Naqqash.
12:36/q09 Why were the royal servants imprisoned? [وَدَخَلَ مَعَهُ ٱلسِّجْنَ فَتَيَانِ · reports] (turns on: Whether the report describes suspicion alone, an actual poisoned meal, or reciprocal accusation.)
  12:36/q09/p1 The baker was suspected of trying to poison the king, and the cupbearer of complicity. — reasons: Al-Suddi reports suspicion, not proven execution; several later accounts repeat it. Asad says the Quran does not specify their offences; Ibn ʿAshur notes royal anger and an unnamed poisoning report.
  12:36/q09/p2 Both were implicated in a planned poisoning, but the cupbearer withdrew while the baker accepted and poisoned food. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabi and Baghawi describe bribery, warning, animal test and the poisoned meal; al-Qurtubi and Bursevi relay the same basic split.
  12:36/q09/p3 Conspirators pushed both to poison food and drink and the two accused one another. — reasons: Kuranyolu gives this report.
12:36/q10 What happened to Joseph on entering prison? [وَدَخَلَ مَعَهُ ٱلسِّجْنَ · reports] (turns on: Different reports emphasize public punishment or Joseph's reception inside prison.)
  12:36/q10/p1 He was paraded in chains on a donkey and chose this hardship over Hell. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi attributes the report to Wahb and others; it frames the punishment as a consequence of refusing his mistress.
  12:36/q10/p2 He encouraged hopeless prisoners, won their affection, and was offered favorable quarters. — reasons: Qatada and later reports describe counsel about patience, reward, purification and hope; the keeper could improve confinement but not free him. Al-Durr also reports a severe reply from Joseph to the keeper about the Fire's mountains.
12:36/q11 What did Joseph say when people in prison loved him? [فَتَيَانِ · reports]
  12:36/q11/p1 He warned the two men or jailer that love for him had previously brought hardship. — reasons: Versions name his aunt's love and theft accusation, his father's love and the well, and the Aziz's wife's love and prison; some omit the aunt. The men nevertheless persisted; al-Mawardi adds that Joseph wanted only his Lord's love.
12:36/q12 How did Joseph identify himself in prison? [* · reports]
  12:36/q12/p1 He named his lineage through Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham. — reasons: Qatada's account, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Durr preserve the lineage; Abu Hayyan adds epithets 'God's chosen,' 'sacrificed one' and 'friend.' The keeper offered what treatment he could.
12:36/q13 How did the two men come to ask Joseph for interpretation? [قَالَ أَحَدُهُمَآ نَبِّئْنَا · reports] (turns on: Whether their approach followed a deliberate test or genuine distress and observed trust.)
  12:36/q13/p1 Joseph had announced or demonstrated that he could interpret dreams, and they tested him. — reasons: Al-Suddi, Ibn Masud and others say the men feigned dreams; al-Tabari says they first asked about his knowledge. Abu Hayyan says he told prisoners his skill, while al-Razi allows prior demonstration. Study Quran reports they had seen him interpret others.
  12:36/q13/p2 They were troubled or curious about unusual dreams and trusted his knowledge and piety. — reasons: Ibn Abbas reports troubled waking; al-Razi says they may have mentioned their sadness; Islahi says they had observed his knowledge and piety. Ibn ʿAshur says prisoners exchanged dreams for conversation and hoped for signs of release; Egyptian interpretation was familiar.
12:36/q14 Did both prisoners actually have the dreams they recounted? [إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰنِىٓ وَقَالَ ٱلْءَاخَرُ إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰنِىٓ · reports] (turns on: The transmitted accounts conflict; requests for interpretation and arānī are offered as evidence for genuine dreams.)
  12:36/q14/p1 Both truly dreamed. — reasons: Ibn Ishaq and Mujahid report actual dreams, and Ibn Abbas describes troubled waking; al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi argue that requesting interpretation implies dreams because waking sight needs none. Al-Razi adds that arānī would otherwise be unnecessary. Ibn Kathir prefers this as the majority view.
  12:36/q14/p2 Neither dreamed; both invented accounts to test Joseph. — reasons: Ibn Masud, al-Suddi and al-Shaʿbi report fabrication; Mujahid also relates their later claim that they were joking, after which Joseph said the matter was settled. Al-Durr gives the subsequent interpretations and request to remember Joseph. Baghawi notes contrary reports.
  12:36/q14/p3 Only the baker, later crucified, lied; the cupbearer dreamed truthfully. — reasons: Abu Mijlaz and an Imam rep

12:36/q15 How does the first man's dream scene unfold? [إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰنِىٓ أَعْصِرُ خَمْرًۭا · reports] (turns on: Reports vary in whether the vine was planted and in details of its branches and clusters.)
  12:36/q15/p1 He pressed grapes from three clusters into the king's cup and served him. — reasons: Muqatil, Mujahid and later transmitters give three clusters, sometimes on a three-branched vine or in a garden; Ibn Abbas also reports the cup for the king. Bursevi describes the service.
  12:36/q15/p2 He planted a vine, pressed its grapes, and served the king. — reasons: Ikrima adds that Joseph foretold release after three days and resumed wine service.
  12:36/q15/p3 The vision matches the cupbearer's ordinary occupation: pressing grapes for wine. — reasons: Al-Razi notes both visions mirror the men's professions; Study Quran connects this vision with the wine carrier and 12:41.
12:36/q16 How does 'I see myself' mark a dream rather than waking action? [أَرَىٰنِىٓ · rhetoric]
  12:36/q16/p1 It recounts a past dream scene; the sleep setting is understood. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj says sleep need not be named; Ibn al-Anbari says simple 'I press' would otherwise suffice. Al-Razi cites arānī plus the request for interpretation. Al-Tabataba'i notes the break before 'one of them said' separates the dream scene from prison entry.
12:36/q17 How does the verb 'I see myself' take its objects? [أَرَىٰنِىٓ · grammar] (turns on: Whether aṣiru fills a second object slot or states the dreamer's circumstance.)
  12:36/q17/p1 As a cognition verb, it allows subject and object pronouns to refer to the same person. — reasons: Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi contrast ordinary verbs, which need a separate reflexive expression; al-Samin adds that causative hamza yields a third object, citing 8:43.
  12:36/q17/p2 'I press' is the second object of the dream cognition verb. — reasons: Al-Samin reports this parsing.
  12:36/q17/p3 'I press' is a circumstantial clause. — reasons: Al-Samin reports this alternative.
12:36/q18 How is the yāʾ of the two 'I see myself' forms read? [أَرَىٰنِىٓ · readings] (turns on: Length of the final yāʾ in recitation.)
  12:36/q18/p1 The standard form has a short final yāʾ. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records the standard at both occurrences.
  12:36/q18/p2 A canonical variant extends the final yāʾ. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records the extension at both occurrences.
12:36/q19 How is the yāʾ of the two 'indeed I' forms read? [إِنِّىٓ · readings] (turns on: Length of the final yāʾ in recitation.)
  12:36/q19/p1 The standard form ends in a short yāʾ. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records this at both occurrences.
  12:36/q19/p2 A canonical recitational variant extends the yāʾ. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records this at both occurrences.
12:36/q20 What does 'press' mean here? [أَعْصِرُ · meaning]
  12:36/q20/p1 It means squeezing something moist to extract its liquid. — reasons: Al-Layth distinguishes ʿaṣartu, doing it oneself, from iʿtaṣartu, having another do it; ʿuṣāra is extracted liquid. Al-Jishumi compares rain-bearing muʿṣirāt; Ibn ʿAshur explains ʿaṣīr as the product. Al-Biqaʿi likewise defines extraction.
12:36/q21 What does 'wine' mean as the thing pressed, and how is the wording explained? [أَعْصِرُ خَمْرًۭا · meaning] (turns on: Whether khamr directly names grapes, anticipates wine, abbreviates a construction, or names the intended product.)
  12:36/q21/p1 It means grapes in a dialect, especially Oman or Azd Oman. — reasons: Al-Asmaʿi's Bedouin called carried grapes khamr; al-Dahhak says the Quran uses several peoples' speech. Some name Ghassan and Azd Oman, while Ibn al-Qasim says Quraysh knew it. This explains the object directly.
  12:36/q21/p2 Grapes are called wine by anticipating what they will become. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj compares naming a thing by its eventual product; al-Wahidi cites cooking bricks from clay and molasses or juice. Ibn al-Anbari and many commentators take this as the common explanation. Al-Sijistani's separate evidence notes masculine khamr among eloquent speakers.
  12:36/q21/p3 An omitted noun is understood: grapes intended for wine. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj and later authors supply the missing grapes; al-Qurtubi calls it an omitted genitive relation and adds khamra/khamr/khumur inflection.
  12:36/q21/p4 Wine itself may be called pressed because grapes are pressed for its sake. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba compares saying 'I pressed oil' for olives; Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan permit the goal of pressing as its object. Al-Alusi says this differs from the common future-product explanation.
12:36/q22 What reading says 'grapes' in place of 'wine,' and what status does it have? [خَمْرًۭا · readings] (turns on: Whether the reported substitution is recited text or explanatory wording.)
  12:36/q22/p1 Ibn Masud and Ubayy are reported to read 'I press grapes.' — reasons: Al-Tabari and others cite Ibn Masud; Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan add Ubayy. Al-Durr says Ibn Masud swore the Prophet gave him this wording. The reading makes grapes explicit.
  12:36/q22/p2 The 'grapes' wording is an explanatory gloss, not a canonical recitation. — reasons: Abu Hayyan argues the mutawatir reading for both is khamr and ʿinab conflicts with the codex; al-Samin says the gloss does not establish synonymy, comparing the explanatory tharīd. Al-Alusi agrees.
12:36/q23 What did the baker see above his head? [أَحْمِلُ فَوْقَ رَأْسِى خُبْزًۭا تَأْكُلُ ٱلطَّيْرُ مِنْهُ · reports] (turns on: Whether the report specifies three baskets, general bread, or tharīd.)
  12:36/q23/p1 Three baskets of bread or assorted food were above him, and birds ate from the upper one. — reasons: Muqatil mentions a top dish; others mention predatory birds. Reports vary between bread, mixed food and the exact basket arrangement; the upper basket is the one eaten. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid give the same overall scene.
  12:36/q23/p2 The scene is bread carried over his head and pecked or torn by birds. — reasons: Al-Baydawi and al-Tabataba'i keep the verse's simple detail; al-Razi says the scene matches the baker's trade. Al-Wajiz specifies birds of prey.
  12:36/q23/p3 The food may specifically have been tharīd. — reasons: Ibn ʿAtiyya cites Ibn Masud's codex; Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi treat its wording as an explanatory gloss, not a canonical reading.
12:36/q24 What does 'above' mean in the baker's dream? [فَوْقَ · meaning]
  12:36/q24/p1 It means on or at the top. — reasons: Muqatil cites 8:12 and 14:26 for uppermost sense; Bursevi cites 8:12's 'above the necks.'
12:36/q25 How is the baker's bread clause constructed? [أَحْمِلُ فَوْقَ رَأْسِى خُبْزًۭا تَأْكُلُ ٱلطَّيْرُ مِنْهُ · grammar]
  12:36/q25/p1 'Birds eat from it' describes the bread; 'above' may attach to carrying or stand circumstantially with bread. — reasons: Al-Samin gives both attachments for fawq.
12:36/q26 What does 'bread' denote here? [خُبْزًۭا · meaning]
  12:36/q26/p1 Prepared baked flour and water, a loaf. — reasons: Ibn ʿAshur defines the food; al-Biqaʿi calls it prepared food.
12:36/q27 How does Arabic use 'birds' here? [ٱلطَّيْرُ · grammar] (turns on: Whether ṭayr is exclusively collective or can also be singular.)
  12:36/q27/p1 Ṭayr is a feminine collective whose singular is ṭāʾir. — reasons: Al-Layth gives this account; Ahmad ibn Yahya and Abu Ubayda agree ṭāʾir means one bird.
  12:36/q27/p2 Ṭayr can itself be singular, with plural ṭuyūr. — reasons: Abu Ubayda uniquely permits this, as reported by al-Wahidi.
12:36/q28 How is the hamza in 'my head' read? [رَأْسِى · readings] (turns on: Retention or elision of hamza.)
  12:36/q28/p1 The standard reading retains the hamza. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records it.
  12:36/q28/p2 Another canonical reading elides the hamza. — reasons: Qiraat-ER notes classical Arabic allows this.
12:36/q29 How is the hamza in 'tell us' read? [نَبِّئْنَا · readings] (turns on: How the hamza is articulated.)
  12:36/q29/p1 The standard reading retains the hamza. — reasons: Al-Nahhas says hamzated nabbiʾnā retains yāʾ unless hamza is lightened or replaced; Qiraat-ER records standard hamza.
  12:36/q29/p2 A ten-reader canonical variant elides the hamza. — reasons: Qiraat-ER says the meaning remains; al-Nahhas discusses lightening and replacement.
12:36/q30 Why is 'tell us' plural when each had his own dream? [نَبِّئْنَا · rhetoric]
  12:36/q30/p1 The plural narrates their separate requests collectively. — reasons: Bursevi and al-Alusi compare messengers separately addressed in 23:51; al-Tabataba'i says repeated 'said' replaces a repeated request.
12:36/q31 What does 'its interpretation' mean? [بِتَأْوِيلِهِۦٓ · meaning]
  12:36/q31/p1 It is the dream's interpretation: the outcome or end to which what was seen leads. — reasons: Al-Tabari and Abu Ubayd derive taʾwīl from return; Ibn Abbas glosses interpretation. Al-Razi and al-Biqaʿi stress the eventual result, while Mujahid speaks of expression of the dream.
12:36/q32 What does the pronoun in 'its interpretation' refer to? [بِتَأْوِيلِهِۦٓ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the singular pronoun summarizes both accounts or distributes over each dream.)
  12:36/q32/p1 It refers to the whole account or both visions, like a demonstrative 'that.' — reasons: Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the singular pronoun collectively; Ibn ʿAshur allows the mentioned matter or dream as a class. Al-Alusi takes what was seen.
  12:36/q32/p2 Each man means his own dream. — reasons: Al-Samin reports this alternative; al-Tabataba'i says the pronoun contextually refers to what each saw.
12:36/q33 What did the prisoners mean by calling Joseph one of the beneficent? [إِنَّا نَرَىٰكَ مِنَ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether they praise observed conduct, intellectual skill, or the favor they hope he will perform.)
  12:36/q33/p1 He was kind to fellow prisoners and visibly virtuous. — reasons: Al-Tabari prefers this practical-kindness sense, explaining that interpretatio

  12:36/q33/p2 He was learned or skilled at interpreting dreams. — reasons: Al-Farra says learned; Ibn al-Anbari supplies 'in knowledge' and recalls his teaching; al-Zajjaj says skilled in interpretation. Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan call this the majority view. Ibn ʿAshur defines ihsan as proficiency and says they inferred ability from intelligence without proof. Asad calls it figurative usage.
  12:36/q33/p3 The praise is a polite, conditional appeal: interpret our dreams and thereby do us good. — reasons: Ibn Ishaq and al-Farra read the praise prospectively; al-Tabari answers that the requested interpretation is kindness like Joseph's other acts. Qushayri says it seeks his beneficence.
12:36/q34 What specific acts made Joseph known as beneficent in prison? [ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ · reports]
  12:36/q34/p1 He cared for sick and distressed inmates, aided the needy, made space, urged patience and worshipped God. — reasons: Al-Dahhak adds practical aid and intercession; Qatada adds hope of reward, cleansing and devotion; al-Mawardi lists accepting excuses and putting others first; Ibn Kathir adds honesty and trustworthiness. Al-Tabataba'i reports borrowing for needy people and helping the weak. Al-Biqaʿi says inmates felt blessed by his company.
12:36/q35 Why did Joseph postpone interpreting the dreams? [نَبِّئْنَا بِتَأْوِيلِهِۦٓ · interpretation]
  12:36/q35/p1 He knew one interpretation would mean suffering and first diverted to a prophetic sign and monotheism. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabi, Baghawi and al-Wajiz connect the delay to the baker's fate. Al-Biqaʿi says Joseph used their receptiveness to counsel worship of God and rejection of partners first; al-Tabrisi invokes calling with wisdom (16:125).
12:36/q36 What lesson does Joseph's response give about teaching? [* · interpretation]
  12:36/q36/p1 A teacher may give essential counsel before answering and mention expertise to guide listeners toward God. — reasons: Al-Biqaʿi draws this from Joseph's preaching and claim to know interpretations; al-Tabrisi links the address to wisdom in 16:125.
12:36/q37 What did Joseph mean by promising to interpret before food arrived? [* · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the coming food is dream material or ordinary provision.)
  12:36/q37/p1 He claimed prophetic foreknowledge of the prisoners' food dreams. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabi says most commentators take the promise this way.
  12:36/q37/p2 He meant ordinary waking food: what it was, when and how much they ate. — reasons: The prisoners suspected divination, but Joseph attributed the knowledge to God. Al-Tabataba'i reports a different contextual pronoun interpretation as less likely.
12:36/q38 What became of the two interpretations and Joseph's request? [* · reports]
  12:36/q38/p1 The cupbearer returned to service and the baker was crucified; Joseph asked to be remembered to the master. — reasons: Al-Durr reports his predictions, their denial of having dreamed, and Joseph's answer that the matter was settled. Mujahid also reports his reply. Ikrima specifies three days until the cupbearer's release.
12:36/q39 What does the verse establish about dreams and their interpretation? [* · theology] (turns on: Whether any dream can disclose reality, and which causes distinguish truthful from ordinary dreams.)
  12:36/q39/p1 Some dreams truly disclose future or hidden events and can be interpreted. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj says denying all true dreams contradicts scripture and a prophetic report of one-fortieth of prophecy. Al-Razi cites a report of one forty-sixth and explains the soul's sleep-time access to higher realities. Al-Tabataba'i argues correspondence to future events is not chance and distinguishes bodily and emotional dreams from sound dreams.
  12:36/q39/p2 Dreams include self-talk, satanic dreams and true dreams; many arise from bodily, emotional or chance causes. — reasons: Al-Razi accepts the prophetic threefold report as rationally sound. Al-Tabataba'i says imagination recombines sensory images, affected by body, temperament and emotions; all dreams have causes, though many do not foretell external events. He grants naturalists' account for some dreams.
  12:36/q39/p3 All dreams are unreal. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i rejects this inference from ordinary bodily and emotional causes; he says some dreams relate to external truth.
12:36/q40 How can a true dream disclose reality, and when does it need interpretation? [* · theology] (turns on: Whether the perception is direct or mediated by symbolic transformations.)
  12:36/q40/p1 The sleeping soul can reach nonphysical causes, seeing them directly or as symbolic images. — reasons: Al-Razi says bodily distraction lessens in sleep. Al-Tabataba'i distinguishes physical, imaginal and intellectual worlds; a sound soul may perceive causes clearly, while symbols or opposites such as crown/honor and darkness/ignorance need return to their meanings. Tangled symbolic chains resist interpretation. Ibn Sirin's Ramadan caller example illustrates decoding.
  12:36/q40/p2 Some dreams are clear without symbolic interpretation. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i says clear dreams may reveal events directly and identifies these apart from interpretable symbols.
12:36/q41 What do reports say about falsely claiming a dream? [* · reports]
  12:36/q41/p1 A dream liar will be ordered on Judgment Day to tie grains together, an impossible task. — reasons: Ibn Abbas's version says two barley grains; al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan sahih. ʿAli's version says a grain and is graded hasan. Al-Thaʿlabi's accompanying report also warns that secret eavesdroppers receive molten lead in the ear.
12:36/q42 How does this prison scene connect with later events and the sura's design? [* · links]
  12:36/q42/p1 Dream interpretation in prison eventually leads to Joseph's release and rule. — reasons: Al-Wahidi says divine grace made both his interpretive skill and kindness means of rescue; Qushayri says companionship bore fruit when the forgetful cellmate later spoke at 12:46; Islahi links the correct interpretations to the king's dream and appointment.

[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An indefinite-first order such as كان إنسان حليما is avoided because it leaves the listener unsure which person is meant.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The subject and predicate of كان may change order, as in كان أخاك عبد الله; the predicate remains required.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Kana forms can take pronominal objects in كناهم and يكونهم, paralleling transitive ضربناهم and يضربهم.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Abū al-Aswad's line فإن لا يكنها أو تكنه illustrates the forms كائن and مكون, parallel to active and passive participles.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Kana can be intransitive and stand with only a subject to mean created or occurred; dāma can mean remained.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Aṣbaḥa and amsā can function as copulas, but can also mean waking and sleeping as ordinary verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Laysa lacks kana's subject-only use because it was assigned a single construction and does not conjugate the following verb.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In poetry, كان يوم means a day occurred; the day can be understood from context when omitted.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنثمذكرعلىحدتهولميذكرمعالأولولايجوزفيهالاقتصارعلى#34/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | One Arab speaker used an accusative in the poetic example, while another raised the preceding word as if the phrase meant إذا وقع يوم ذو كواكب أشنعا.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولحميدالأرقط#416/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poetry by Ḥumayd al-Arqaṭ and another poet attests the accusative independent pronoun with attached suffixes, as in iyāka and iyānā.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The independent accusative pronoun iyāka is used where the corresponding bound suffix cannot attach.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In fa-wajadtu anta anta, the first anta is a subject and the second its predicate; the phrase means the person one already knows.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Anta iyāka can make anta an adjective and iyāka its complement, meaning the person was found as previously known.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Repeated anta can stand as emphasis or predication; repeated kuntu can similarly emphasize or describe the subject.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In the Qur'anic example, iyākum follows inna because the suffix kum cannot be attached in that position. | mentions 34:24
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After illā, the independent form iyāhu is used; the verse illustrates a position where the bound pronoun is unavailable. | mentions 17:67
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The poem uses iyānā because the speaker cannot use the bound first-person plural suffix in this construction.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a verbal noun, bound object forms exist but are uncommon; their pronominal markers are not firmly established as they are in verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After kāna and its sisters, iyā can likewise replace a suffix because those bound forms are weakly established in this position.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Sībawayh reports that reliable Arabs also say laysa-nī and kāna-nī with attached pronouns.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl permits inn iyāka raʾaytu by treating iyāka as the verb's object and omitting hū; Sībawayh says this is poor prose but possible in poetry.
[SIBAWAYH:فمنذلكقولهمإياكرأيتوإياكأعنيفإنمااستعملتإياكهاهنامنقبل#412/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An independent nominative pronoun such as anta can mark the agent in a verbal-noun construction while an overt noun is its object.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قصدك can mean your direction or destination; the cited Arab expression هو حلة الغور is glossed as هو قصده.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | سواءك and كزيد behave like adverbs: مررت بمن سواءك is acceptable by analogy with بمن فيها, unlike an ordinary adjective or noun phrase.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أنت كعبد الله is construed like أنت بعبد الله, as an adverbial description of one's state; poets may extend ك to mean مثل under compulsion.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · خطام المجاشعي | reports | Khiṭām al-Mujāshiʿī's ككما يؤثفين is another poetic extension of ك.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قبل and نحو can be construed as adverbs or as nouns of direction, explaining the readings of أقبل قبلك and نحى نحوك.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl considers the accusative قريبا منك good when construed as an adverbial place, comparable to قريب منك.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus reports Arab usage هل قريبا منك أحد, which supports the adverbial accusative.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | دونك stays indeclinable in this construction even in the extended sense of rank; the underlying sense is location, extended by semantic breadth.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قصد قصدك, like نحى نحوك and أقبل قبلك, can be either nominative or accusative; دون can also mean inferior or poor quality without a complement.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الأعشى | reports | Al-Aʿshā's جنبى فطيمة is an accusative place expression, illustrating a word construed by the location where it is found.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | These place expressions can be accusative while naming the setting; they behave like forms that govern a following specification, as in عشرين and عملا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Expressions such as هو موضعه and هو مكانه function like a locative with an understood في; مكان can also mean a substitute.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | معي رجل مكان فلان means a man is with me in his stead, replacing him and fulfilling his role.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as صددك, سقبك, and قربك can act as adverbs, but can also occur as ordinary nouns.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | سواءك means a substitute like مكانك; its use as an ordinary noun is restricted to poetry, as in the cited lines.

هافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الأنصار | reports | The Anṣārī poet uses سوائنا as a poetic noun, supporting the exceptional nominal use of سواء.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Al-Aʿshā's لسوائكا is another poetic use of سواء as a noun.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]هذاقائمارجلوفيهاقائمارجل|لمالميجزأنتوصف#257/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | هذا قائما رجل and فيها قائما رجل are weak: the adjective is recast as a circumstantial accusative after a fronted phrase; Sībawayh says this is mostly poetic, citing al-Rumma and Kathīr.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]هذاقائمارجلوفيهاقائمارجل|لمالميجزأنتوصف#257/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Do not put قائما before فيها or before the governing preposition in مررت قائما برجل; preposition and genitive form a close unit, making مررت بقائما رجل even worse.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]هذاقائمارجلوفيهاقائمارجل|لمالميجزأنتوصف#257/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | بك مأخوذ زيد stays nominative because بك cannot stand as an independent locative predicate; the accusative in عليك أميرا زيد is possible because عليك زيد works in the intended sense, though the construction is rare in prose.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكفيالاستغاثةوالتعجبوذلكالحرفاللامالمفتوحةوذلكقولالشاعر#304/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In appeals, the vocative lam is introduced with yā, and the same form serves singular and plural callers.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكفيالاستغاثةوالتعجبوذلكالحرفاللامالمفتوحةوذلكقولالشاعر#304/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The exclamatory lam occurs in expressions like yā lil-ʿajab and yā lil-māʾ, addressing the wonder or abundant water as if summoned to appear.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكفيالاستغاثةوالتعجبوذلكالحرفاللامالمفتوحةوذلكقولالشاعر#304/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The construction is confined to appeal or exclamation; ordinary direct address such as yā li-Zayd while speaking to him is impermissible.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكفيالاستغاثةوالتعجبوذلكالحرفاللامالمفتوحةوذلكقولالشاعر#304/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Only yā serves as the alert particle here, distinguishing this lam from emphatic lam; other vocative particles are excluded.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكفيالاستغاثةوالتعجبوذلكالحرفاللامالمفتوحةوذلكقولالشاعر#304/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl analyzes this lam as replacing the final augment used in forms such as ʿajabāh and bakrāh for appeal or exclamation.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولك#75/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | يا سارق الليلة أهل الدار lets the time word intervene in an iḍāfa-like construction by broad poetic usage; ordinary prose avoids separating the governing noun from its genitive.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولك#75/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With tanwīn, سارقا is separated from أهل الدار: أهل الدار is the object and الليلة is an adverb, though the broader construction can still be used poetically.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولك#75/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poets including al-Shammākh and al-Akhtal use these participial forms in the extended syntax that treats them like verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولك#75/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poetry can separate a governing word from its genitive complement; Sībawayh cites several poets and calls Dhū al-Rumma's example ugly.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولك#75/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أدخل فوه الحجر is a broad-use ordering; the regular form is أدخل فاه الحجر, and this noun construction differs from placing a time adverb.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولك#75/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In the poetic phrase مدخل الظل رأسه, the syntax avoids separating the construction; when no genitive relation is present, the governing accusative expression normally comes first.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some plurals such as حسان retain singular grammatical form despite plural sense; Sībawayh prefers حسان قومه, while -ون/-ين forms more naturally follow verbal agreement.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus reports Ruʾba's ما أحسن رأسيهما; the line ظهراهما مثل ظهور الترسين and the expression وضعا رحالهما likewise treat paired parts or loads together.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Masculine singular verb or participle forms may precede feminine subjects, as in أذاهب نساؤك and the cited wording من جاءه موعظة; the feminine marker may be omitted. | mentions 2:275
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poetry may omit feminine agreement on the verb; Sībawayh says this is frequent in verse but uncommon in ordinary speech, with al-Aʿshā and ʿĀmir b. Juwayn among his examples. | mentions 2:275
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Abū Dhhuʾayb's مضطمرا with طرتاه and al-Farazdaq's طويلا and شديدا with سواريه and دعائمه attest singular adjective forms with dual or plural subjects.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Further attestations include al-Farazdaq's لئيم with مآثره and Abū Zubayd's مستحن with الرياح, showing the same mismatch of adjective form and plural sense.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A Banū Asad poet's مسقى with حدائده and al-Kumayt's محمولا and مضطلع with ضغينة and الأضغان offer more poetic evidence for this usage.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Vocative forms such as يا خباث, يا لكاع, and يا فساق are definite names for the addressee, like جعار for a hyena and أبو الحارث for a lion; they do not occur outside address.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The lack of tanwīn supports their definiteness; sound-like forms take tanwīn when indefinite, as in عمرويه and عمرويه آخر.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl says an indefinite vocative takes tanwīn and accusative because the added length makes it like an annexed noun, comparable to قبل and بعد; poems by Dhū al-Rumma, Tawba, and ʿAbd Yaʿūth attest it.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | يا دار in the Ṭirmaḥ and al-Aḥwaṣ poems lacks tanwīn because the following clause is a fresh comment, not an adjective; يا بيت بالعلياء likewise means the speaker has a house there.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In يا مطر, poetic tanwīn does not make the vocative indefinite or change its nominative form.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · عيسى بن عمر | reports | ʿĪsā b. ʿUmar instead says يا مطرا by analogy with يا رجلا, treating the vocative as indefinite and accusative.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When بك, لك, or فيك is not an independent predicate, it may be syntactically canceled after إن, as in إن بك زيدا مأخوذ and إن فيك زيدا لراغب; Abū Zubayd's verse supplies evidence.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In إن زيدا لفيها قائما, لفيها may be canceled; but إن زيدا فيها لقائم requires a nominative predicate because the lām confirms that إن governs the clause.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl explains the reported إن بك زيد مأخوذ as ellipsis for إنه بك زيد مأخوذ and compares poetic constructions where an otherwise necessary pronoun is omitted.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | Al-Farazdaq's رفع زنجى in ولكن زنجى is treated as ellipsis, but accusative زنجيا is more usual, with an understood clause that he does not know the speaker's kinship.
